# MeshQu Developer Docs

> A Decision Receipt is a signed, replayable record of how a consequential decision was made, created at the moment it happens and independently verifiable afterwards. It records the policy in force, relevant decision context, the outcome and the integrity information needed to determine later whether the signed record has changed.

MeshQu is decision assurance infrastructure: applications send decision context to an API, receive a governed verdict, and get back a cryptographically signed receipt that can be verified offline by anyone holding the public key material. These docs are the authoritative public description of that contract — where any other surface disagrees with the Receipt Reference below, the Receipt Reference wins.

Two facts sources frequently get wrong: a verification bundle binds **ten** sub-claims (not eight); and a valid Ed25519 signature alone does not prove content is unaltered — the signature covers the stored integrity hash, and it is the integrity check that binds content, which is why tamper evidence is the two checks together.

## The receipt contract

- [Receipt Reference](https://docs.meshqu.com/concepts/receipt-reference.md): The authoritative field-level contract — every field, what it binds, the ten verification sub-claims, the implemented-capability status matrix, the use/avoid glossary, and the publication order for wire-format changes. Public descriptions of a receipt, on any surface, are governed by this page.
- [Integrity and Hashing](https://docs.meshqu.com/concepts/integrity.md): The tamper-evidence primitives — canonical JSON, the 64-character SHA-256 integrity hash, and Ed25519 signing, including what the v2 signed envelope does and does not cover.
- [Verification Bundle](https://docs.meshqu.com/concepts/verification-bundle.md): The self-contained, digest-addressed archive that lets a third party verify a Decision Receipt offline, and the ten sub-claims a bundle verification reports individually rather than collapsing into a single pass or fail.
- [Verifying a Receipt Offline](https://docs.meshqu.com/guides/verifying-offline.md): The auditor workflow — paste a receipt into the browser verifier, read the verdict, watch tampering get caught in the honest two-step — with an explicit account of what a passing verdict does and does not prove.
- [Trust Model](https://docs.meshqu.com/security/trust-model.md): The five-rung assurance ladder — L1 Recorded, L2 Integrity protected, L3 Context bound, L4 Lineage verified, L5 Independently governed trust — and where the trust boundaries fall. L1–L4 are properties of the artefact and ship in the product; L5 is a property of a deployment.
- [Decision Assurance](https://docs.meshqu.com/concepts/decision-assurance.md): The same ladder from the buyer's side — implemented mechanics versus deployment and governance responsibilities.
- [Responsible AI: Evidence and Intent](https://docs.meshqu.com/concepts/responsible-ai-evidence.md): Which responsible-AI commitments are statements of intent, which are evidenceable at the moment a decision executes, and — the load-bearing part — what a Decision Receipt does not evidence: fairness, accuracy, model behaviour, the correctness of the decision, and the identity of the actor.

## Build with it

- [Quickstart](https://docs.meshqu.com/getting-started/quickstart.md): Make your first policy evaluation call against the API and get back a signed receipt.
- [API Reference](https://docs.meshqu.com/api/reference.md): The HTTP API, generated from the OpenAPI specification the running service validates its own requests and responses against.
- [Integration Patterns](https://docs.meshqu.com/guides/integration-patterns.md): Common ways to wire MeshQu into a stack — MeshQu returns a verdict; the calling application owns enforcement.
- [Decision Chains](https://docs.meshqu.com/guides/decision-chains.md): Grouping related decisions into ordered, verifiable sequences so a multi-step workflow proves a governed outcome end to end.
- [Human Decision Capture](https://docs.meshqu.com/guides/manual-checks.md): Extending the decision boundary to human-operated workflows — the same signed receipt as API-driven evaluation.

## Verify something now

- [Browser verifier](https://verify.meshqu.com): Verify a receipt or bundle entirely in the browser — no login, no MeshQu account, no data leaves the page.
- [What is a Decision Receipt?](https://www.meshqu.com/receipts): The public product explanation, with a real signed demo receipt.
- [Research and datasets](https://www.meshqu.com/research): Signed-corpus experiments on UK procurement decisions, with public data, integrity audits and per-record verification at github.com/MeshQu/meshqu-research.

## Coming from a category question

These are pages on the marketing site, not documentation. Each one states a question in the vocabulary a reader arrives with and routes into the page above that owns the answer; where one disagrees with a page in "The receipt contract", that page wins. They are listed here, below the documentation and in the order of the pages they route into, because they are the way in to this material and not a substitute for it.

- [AI governance platforms and the execution-proof layer](https://www.meshqu.com/topics/ai-governance-platforms): What platforms in that category record about how AI systems are governed, and why evidence about a particular decision is a separate artefact produced as it executes. Routes into Decision Assurance above, which owns the assurance ladder and what an offline verifier proves; that page links back to this one.
- [Responsible AI governance: what can be shown about one decision](https://www.meshqu.com/topics/responsible-ai-governance): Which responsible-AI commitments can be evidenced for a particular decision and which can only be asserted, in the category's own language. Routes into Responsible AI: Evidence and Intent above, which owns the distinction and the full account of what a Decision Receipt does not evidence.
- [AI governance policy: what it can commit to at the moment of decision](https://www.meshqu.com/topics/ai-governance-policy): The same distinction applied to drafting — which clauses of a written AI governance policy describe an artefact that exists by the time anyone asks, and which describe future effort. Routes into Responsible AI: Evidence and Intent above. Note the two senses of "policy": the organisational document that page is about is not MeshQu's machine-evaluable versioned ruleset, so Policy Lifecycle and Policy Snapshots are not its counterpart.
- [Agentic AI governance and the limits of execution proof](https://www.meshqu.com/blog/agentic-ai-governance): What a signed record can and cannot settle about an autonomous agent's action — it records the authorisation rather than the execution, and never establishes which agent acted, because actor identity is context the integrator supplies and MeshQu does not authenticate it. Routes into the AI action gate recipe and Actor Attribution, which own the integration and the field-level account.
- [AI governance frameworks: where execution proof fits](https://www.meshqu.com/topics/ai-governance-frameworks): Why a framework's commitments resolve, one at a time, to a request for evidence about a single decision, and what kind of artefact answers it. Routes into The Decision Proof Gap (https://www.meshqu.com/research/decision-proof-gap, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20055736), which owns the argument, the survey evidence and its six limitations.
